title: Skilled and Motivated Work Team Output

lessons.title: Assessing the team's skills and motivation
lessons.html:
Assessing the team's skills and motivation

In this work experience module you lead a real team in the orchard or vineyard over a production period, with the aim of producing a skilled, motivated team that reaches its output and quality goals. You will collect evidence in a portfolio signed by your mentor.

Skills assessment

Build or update a skills matrix for your team. For each worker and each key operation - pruning, thinning, canopy work, picking, irrigation checks, spraying, tractor driving, first aid - record whether they are competent, in training or not trained. Observe each worker on the job rather than relying only on what they say. Note who could become a team leader or trainer.

Performance baseline

From job cards and quality sheets, record each team's current productivity and quality: trees pruned per day, bins per picker, quality sample pass rates, damage percentages. Also record attendance and safety incidents. These numbers are your starting point.

Understanding motivation

Talk to workers informally and listen. Ask what makes the work easier or harder, what they would change, and what they hope for in their work. Common themes on farms include:

  • Fair and transparent pay and counts.
  • Respectful treatment by supervisors.
  • Reliable transport and facilities in the field.
  • Good tools and PPE.
  • Recognition and chances to learn and grow.
  • Job security and fair allocation of work.

Identifying gaps

Compare skills, performance and motivation findings with what the season requires. List the main gaps: for example, not enough trained pruners for the winter workload, low picking quality in one team, or high absenteeism linked to transport problems. Discuss the list with your mentor and agree priorities.

lessons.title: Developing skills in the team
lessons.html:
Developing skills in the team

Training plan

Create a simple training plan for the period: which workers, which skills, by when, who will train them and how competence will be checked. Prioritise skills needed for the next operations in the production calendar.

On-the-job training method

  1. Prepare: choose a suitable block, tools and a small group.
  2. Explain: what the task is, why it matters, the standard.
  3. Demonstrate: do it slowly, step by step, while they watch.
  4. Practise: each learner does it while you watch and guide.
  5. Check: assess against the standard; repeat until competent.
  6. Follow up: check again over the next days.

Using experienced workers

Pair learners with experienced, patient workers as buddies. Train your best workers to become on-the-job trainers - this builds their pride and spreads skills quickly.

Safety-critical skills

Some tasks need formal training and authorisation before a worker may do them alone: tractor and forklift driving, chemical mixing and application, first aid, working at height on platforms. Arrange formal courses with accredited providers through the farm and AgriSETA where relevant, and keep certificates on file.

Training records

Record each training session: date, topic, trainer, attendees and result. Update the skills matrix. Audits often check training records, especially for hygiene, chemical handling and safety.

Measuring training results

After training, compare the workers' productivity and quality with the baseline. A good training programme should show fewer quality failures and faster work within a few weeks.

Remember that training also builds motivation. Workers who gain new skills often feel more valued and are more likely to return in the next season.

lessons.title: Motivating the team and achieving output
lessons.html:
Motivating the team and achieving output

Setting and sharing goals

Agree daily and weekly team goals that include output, quality and safety. Display them on a board at the shed or share them at the morning briefing. Report progress daily so the team can see how they are doing.

Actions that motivate

  • Fix practical barriers quickly: transport, tools, water, toilets, bin supply.
  • Make pay counts transparent and correct errors immediately.
  • Recognise good work publicly and specifically.
  • Use incentive schemes fairly, rewarding quality as well as speed.
  • Give responsibility to those who are ready, such as team leader roles.
  • Treat everyone with respect and apply rules consistently.
  • Listen to ideas and act on good ones.

Dealing with low output

When a team or worker falls short, find the cause before acting. Is it skill, tools, block conditions, health, personal problems or attitude? Coach and support first. Where there is a pattern of unwillingness after support, follow the farm's disciplinary process with HR.

Team spirit

Celebrate achievements such as finishing a block on time or an injury-free month. Encourage teams to help each other. Deal with conflict early and fairly.

Measuring the outcome

At the end of the period, compare with the baseline: productivity, quality pass rates, attendance, incidents and number of workers competent in each skill. Ask workers for feedback on what helped them most.

Portfolio report

Your report should show the baseline, the gaps you found, your training and motivation actions, the results, and what you learnt about leading people. Include the updated skills matrix and training records.

Key points

  • Assess skills by observation and record them in a skills matrix.
  • Set a baseline for productivity, quality, attendance and safety.
  • Train with explain - demonstrate - practise - check, and record it.
  • Motivate by removing barriers, fair pay counts, recognition and respect.
  • Find the cause of low output and coach before discipline.
